summary: On Saturday, the Senate approved a short-term funding measure by a 90-6 vote to fund federal agencies through Dec. 11, averting a potentially chaotic government shutdown during campaign season.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune prioritized the deal nearly two months before the Sept. 30 fiscal deadline to allow senators a five-week recess for reelection campaigns, still recovering from two historic shutdowns this past year.

Senator Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Democrats negotiated provisions blocking new grant regulations opposed by nearly 500,000 public commenters, while also preventing Border Patrol transfers and rejecting the White House's $1 billion battleship request.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer attacked the battleship proposal, saying "The only person who wants these golden ships is Donald Trump so he can slap his name on them," while the White House Office of Management and Budget defended its grant review as improving accountability.

The bill retains a one-month delay on intoxicating hemp products despite Senator Ted Budd's unsuccessful effort to strip it, citing a nearly 10-fold increase in cannabis emergency room visits by minors since 2017; the House must approve when members return from recess.
title: Source Icon

summary: The Senate voted 50–49 to confirm Todd Blanche as U.S. Attorney General, ending a contentious confirmation fight and officially installing President Donald Trump's former criminal defense lawyer atop the Department of Justice.
Sen. Bill Cassidy provided the decisive swing vote after declaring his support on the floor, while Republican Sens. Susan Collins and Lisa Murkowski joined all Democrats in opposing the nomination.

The pre-dawn 4:31 a.m. vote took place immediately before the Senate adjourned for a five-week recess, granting Blanche full confirmation after serving in an acting capacity since Trump removed former AG Pam Bondi in April.

Confirmation prospects were stalled for weeks over a controversial $1.8 billion "anti-weaponization fund" and tax immunity provisions stemming from a DOJ settlement with Trump over his leaked IRS records.

Blanche secured key Republican votes by offering written assurances, officially rescinding the payout fund and clarifying that tax audit immunity applied only to existing claims and did not protect against future tax filings.
title: Senate narrowly approves Todd Blanche as AG, capping tough confirmation fight

summary: President Donald Trump renewed his attempt to remove Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook on Friday, reviving an effort the Supreme Court blocked in June to preserve the central bank's independence.

White House Deputy Chief of Staff Dan Scavino sent a letter dated August 5 to Cook, stating the President is "considering" her removal due to unproven mortgage fraud allegations raised by Bill Pulte, director of the Federal Housing Finance Agency.

The Supreme Court's 5-4 ruling in June blocked the initial firing, finding Trump failed to provide procedural protections; the White House now demands Cook respond within 21 days to satisfy the court's mandate.

Cook, the first Black woman to serve as a Federal Reserve governor, denied wrongdoing and maintained the allegations are "a manufactured pretext" for monetary policy differences, noting she has not been charged with any crime.

Chief Justice John Roberts warned in the June opinion that allowing the President to fire Cook "would in effect transform the Federal Reserve's for-cause protection into at-will employment," undermining the Nation's central banking independence from political pressure.
title: Trump Moving Forward with Attempt to Fire Fed's Lisa Cook After Supreme Court Ruling

summary: On Friday, the U.S. Senate passed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 by an 86-11 vote, targeting Russian energy revenues and extending Iran sanctions through 2031.

Championed by the late Senator Lindsey Graham, the bill aims to increase economic pressure on Russia's war in Ukraine, as Graham believed targeting Moscow's energy income was essential to forcing diplomatic resolution.

President Donald Trump would gain authority to impose tariffs of up to 100% on major purchasers of Russian oil and gas, including China and India, with exemptions for nations importing less than 15% of their gas from Russia.

House lawmakers reconvene August 31 to consider the legislation, though Representatives Gregory Meeks and Don Beyer warned that granting broad tariff authority could harm American consumers and weaponize trade policy.
Momentum surged following Graham's death as lawmakers honored his legacy, and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy welcomed the vote as a critical move to increase pressure on Russia and end the conflict.
title: Senate passes sanctions bill on Russia and Iran named for late Sen. Lindsey Graham

summary: On Friday, a divided D.C. Circuit Court panel ruled 2-1 that President Donald Trump must halt above-ground construction of his $400 million White House ballroom, finding the project requires congressional approval.
The National Trust for Historic Preservation sued the administration last year after Trump demolished the historic East Wing without congressional authorization, challenging the project's legality.
Judges wrote that each president is a "temporary tenant," not an owner of the White House, stating "Whether or not a massive ballroom should be constructed is for Congress to decide."
The court granted a 14-day stay allowing the Trump administration to seek Supreme Court review, while permitting continued underground work on security installations and bunkers beneath the site.
Trump-Appointed Judge Neomi Rao dissented, calling the injunction a "blatant abuse of discretion" and arguing the project fell within the president's authority to improve the Executive Residence.
title: Appeals court rules Trump must get approval from Congress on ballroom, ordering halt to construction

summary: On Friday, Sen. Bill Cassidy announced he will vote to confirm Todd Blanche as U.S. attorney general, keeping President Donald Trump's nominee's confirmation on track.
Sens. Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska announced their opposition this week, both citing what they described as the politicization of the Justice Department.

Cassidy, who voted to convict Trump in his 2021 impeachment trial, spent weeks questioning the nominee's independence; after meeting privately with Blanche, he stated he was "not entirely satisfied" but would support him.

With Sen. Mitch McConnell absent due to hospitalization, Blanche cannot afford further Republican defections; Cassidy's decisive vote prevents the confirmation from collapsing after Collins and Murkowski's opposition.

Blanche, the acting attorney general, faced criticism for defending Trump in the New York criminal trial, while Cassidy blamed both parties for the "apparent lawfare" and weaponization of the Justice Department.
title: Cassidy backs Blanche for attorney general, clearing way for confirmation

The campaign's video included a caption sarcastically suggesting Swift would be 'super excited' her song was used, following years of public friction between the singer and President Trump.
Variety noted that Team Trump's account, which has approximately 14 million followers, also had audio removed from videos using Swift's songs 'Father Figure' and 'Opalite' following similar usage.
While neither the campaign nor Swift officially explained the removal, fans celebrated the move, as Swift's control over her music masters provides her distinct leverage to restrict platform usage.
This incident adds to a long list of artists, including Ariana Grande and The Rolling Stones, who have objected to the Trump campaign using their music without authorization in political messaging.
title: Taylor Swift's 'August' Removed From Donald Trump TikTok Post that Joked She Would Be "Super Excited" About Its Use

summary: On Saturday, incumbent U.S. Rep. Ed Case defeated state Sen. Jarrett Keohokalole in the Democratic primary for Hawai'i's 1st Congressional District, winning 57.3% to 34.2% according to official tallies.

The contest drew national attention pitting an established incumbent against a younger, more progressive challenger, with Keohokalole positioning himself as a changemaker while Case emphasized his legislative seniority and committee experience.

Keohokalole repeatedly criticized Case for voting for an early version of the SAVE Act and remaining silent on immigration enforcement, while Case raised about $1 million largely from defense and sugar industry political action committees.

While Case spent election day sign-waving alone through the district, Keohokalole hosted a watch party at Sacred Hearts Academy with supporters and Tahitian dancers that grew quiet as early results came in.
In the separate 2nd Congressional District race, U.S. Rep. Jill Tokuda secured 84% of the vote and will face Republican Brenton Awa in the November general election.
title: Moderate Democrat in Hawaii Defeats Progressive House Challenger

The legislation seeks to create a comprehensive federal rulebook for the crypto industry, defining which regulators oversee digital tokens; it requires 60 votes to clear the Senate's cloture process.

Democrats continue demanding restrictions on officials' crypto ventures, citing reports that President Donald Trump earned more than $1.4 billion from family projects last year, leaving negotiations fluid on this ethics provision.

With only three weeks of Senate session next month, the bill navigates a crowded legislative agenda alongside federal funding, Russia sanctions, and nominations as Senate leaders pursue bipartisan support.
If the partisan rift persists, the Clarity Act is unlikely to pass this year, potentially forcing the industry to reset its legislative strategy when the new Congress convenes next year.

summary: On Saturday, Delta Flight 2204 returned to Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport shortly after takeoff following reports of fumes in the cockpit, according to the airline.
The Boeing 757 departed Atlanta at 7:23 a.m. for Orlando when the crew declared an emergency after smoke appeared in the flight deck, prompting the immediate return.
All 199 passengers and six crew members evacuated the aircraft on a taxiway using emergency slides, with no injuries reported following the emergency landing.
Ground crews transported travelers by bus back to the terminal, where Delta is re-accommodating them on a replacement aircraft to complete their trip to Florida.
Maintenance teams remain on-site to inspect the grounded plane for the cause of the fumes. Delta stated, "Safety is paramount at Delta, and we apologize to our customers.
title: Delta flight makes emergency landing in Atlanta, no injuries reported

summary: On Saturday, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement said it expects every officer and agent in the field to be equipped with a body-worn camera by the end of August, a rapid expansion providing an unprecedented visual record of enforcement operations.
Heightened scrutiny follows fatal shootings in Maine and Houston involving ICE officers that were not recorded on body cameras, highlighting accountability gaps the agency now seeks to address.

Acting Director David J. Venturella said ICE is "committed to transparency and accountability," defending policies that restrict footage release to protect investigations and privacy as consistent with other federal law enforcement agencies.

Venturella disputed reports that the policy was "mischaracterized," arguing leadership retains discretion to withhold footage when in the agency's "best interests" after serious injury or death, as the Associated Press report focused on.

Transparency concerns persist after Customs and Border Protection failed to release footage of a January fatal shooting in Minneapolis involving Alex Pretti; whether the public will see future ICE footage remains largely at the agency's discretion.
title: ICE says it expects to equip every field officer with body cameras by the end of August

summary: Two drivers filed a class action lawsuit earlier this week in U.S. District Court of California's Western division, alleging the raised metallic AMG logo on front seats is reasonably expected to contact an occupant's upper back, neck, or shoulder.

Lahijani reported second-degree burns on May 31 after entering his leased 2026 Mercedes -AMG E-Class wearing a tank top, with a board-certified dermatologist documenting the injury as AMG inscribed on his skin.

Roughly six weeks later, Chatsworth resident Karendeep Karina Bath received similar burns while wearing a sleeveless top; a mark in the shape of the AMG logo darkened and became visible on her skin, consistent with a thermal contact burn.

Plaintiffs seek compensation for medical expenses, pain, suffering, and emotional distress, alongside costs for Mercedes to remove the logo from other owners' vehicles. Mercedes-Benz could not be reached immediately for comment.

Mercedes-Benz USA and parent company Daimer agreed to pay $149.6 million in December to settle allegations the automaker secretly installed emission-control devices in more than 211,000 diesel vehicles between 2008 and 2016.
title: Two drivers of Mercedes AMG cars file class action lawsuit over an alleged burn hazard in its logo

Reports of the disruption began around 2:30 p.m., with complaints peaking an hour later as more than 13,300 users reported being unable to make or receive phone calls, according to Downdetector.
Verizon engineers were deployed to address the disruption, and the company stated it is "making progress on an issue impacting voice services for some wireless customers" to CNBC.

Customers from other carriers, including AT&T and T-Mobile, also experienced call failures according to Downdetector, while Verizon recommended impacted users restart their devices to restore service.
The company directed users to its website for real-time outage updates, though Verizon did not provide a specific reason for the service disruption as of Saturday evening.
title: Verizon Users Report Phone Service Outage Across US

summary: The United States Embassy announced on Friday that official activities will partially resume in Michoacan's "avocado belt" on Saturday, easing a suspension that had halted critical export inspections due to security concerns.

Security threats prompted the United States to suspend government operations on Wednesday, halting avocado export inspections after violence linked to the arrest of alleged cartel leader Alfonso Fernandez Magallon.
President Claudia Sheinbaum said Mexico is coordinating with the Embassy to guarantee safety, with more than 1,500 soldiers and National Guard personnel deployed to the region.
The Mexican Hass Avocado Association stated on Thursday that the brief pause is not expected to significantly impact near-term sales, as existing inventories should meet United States demand.

United States avocado inspections were also temporarily suspended in 2022 and 2024 following similar security incidents. The Embassy stated it will continue to evaluate conditions and adjust operations as appropriate.
title: U.S. partially resumes avocado inspections in Mexico

summary: The Friday morning crash of a Sikorsky Skycrane in Utah's Fishlake National Forest ignited a fire that merged with an existing blaze, trapping the wreckage inside the fire perimeter and preventing responders from accessing the site.

Officials prioritized safety, deciding not to place additional lives at risk until the Widemouth 2 Fire is more under control; the blaze has now scorched nearly 174 square miles after consuming the initial crash site.

While The National Interagency Fire Center reported the pilot and crew member were fatally injured, officials have not officially confirmed the status of the two people aboard due to the inaccessible crash site and ongoing fire activity.
Investigators plan to examine the wreckage once the site becomes safe; The National Transportation Safety Board cautioned that determining the crash cause will likely take a year or more to conclude.

Dangerous conditions persist across Western states, where concurrent wildfires have forced evacuations of more than 20,000 people in British Columbia and caused the death of 47-year-old Jason Ensign in Oregon.
title: Dangerous wildfire keeps crews from reaching helicopter crash in Utah

Right-Leaning coverage similarly emphasizes practical experimentation, sensors, and “crucial ocean data,” portraying the University of Delaware project as a useful forecasting tool.

The center’s vivid references to “killer shark,” “ tornado -tossed predators,” and “objects of summer fear” create a cultural contrast between menace and utility; the right largely de-emphasizes that framing.

summary: University of Delaware researchers are testing whether sharks can serve as mobile ocean-data observers, deploying electronic sensors to monitor conditions informing hurricane forecasts along the U.S. East Coast.

While oceanographers have long used animal-borne sensors on elephant seals in polar regions, Aaron Carlisle, principal investigator at the School of Marine Science and Policy, noted sharks are abundant and widely distributed, making them ideal research candidates.

Tags attached to dorsal fins transmit data via satellite whenever sharks surface. Carlisle describes the tagging process as operating "like a pit crew," ensuring the procedure takes less than five minutes to minimize animal stress.

By measuring the ocean's mixed layer heat content, sensors provide critical data on storm intensity drivers. This information could offer communities from North Carolina to Massachusetts more reliable hurricane warnings, increasing coastal resilience.

The project also helps reframe public perception of sharks beyond "absurdly dramatic" pop culture portrayals. Carlisle noted that demonstrating how these animals can assist human safety creates a "win-win situation" for conservation and public preparedness.
title: Scientists turn to sharks to improve hurricane predictions

summary: On Friday, Nvidia announced plans to invest up to $3 billion in Lancium, a power infrastructure developer behind the Stargate data center campus in Texas, according to The Information.
Lancium owns the 1,000-acre Lancium Clean Campus in Abilene, Texas, which serves as the first operational site for the Stargate initiative, according to reports.

The chipmaker will invest an initial $2 billion for a roughly 20% stake in the Blackstone-backed company, with an enterprise value of around $10 billion. An additional $1 billion may follow if grid hookup thresholds are met.

Stargate is a joint venture formed by SoftBank, OpenAI, and Oracle; President Donald Trump announced the project in January, estimating a total investment of up to $500 billion for artificial intelligence infrastructure.
The capital is expected to help Lancium expand its operations as the company explores a potential initial public offering in 2027, according to reports.
title: Nvidia to invest up to $3 billion in Stargate data center developer Lancium, the Information reports

summary: On Friday, a U.S. official told Reuters that progress has been made in talks between Iran and Oman on reopening the Strait of Hormuz , with Washington expecting an agreement soon to restore commercial oil shipments.

Before the United States and Israel launched the war on Iran on February 28, about one out of every five barrels of oil consumed worldwide transited the Strait. Iran subsequently used the conflict to justify charging tolls and firing on tankers.

Abu Dhabi National Oil Company reported Friday that 15 of its vessels were struck in unprovoked attacks while transiting the Strait since the conflict began, killing one crew member and wounding 20 others.
In Mecca on Friday, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, and Turkey signed a joint defense agreement stipulating that an armed attack against any one nation would be regarded as an attack on all three.

Analysts warn that internal fissures between Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps may complicate peace efforts, though Central Command reported no strikes on Iran since July 29.
title: US expects Iran to ensure safe oil flow through Strait of Hormuz: Vance

summary: Louisiana Health Department officials reported Thursday that nine people contracted Vibrio vulnificus in 2026, with five deaths resulting from the flesh-eating bacteria found in warm coastal waters.

The bacteria exists naturally in warm coastal waters and infects individuals with exposed open wounds and underlying health conditions; cases typically rise from May to October when water temperatures warm.
According to the CDC, infection occurs through contaminated shellfish or exposed wounds in brackish water; prevention requires avoiding saltwater with open wounds and thoroughly cooking seafood.
This year's five fatalities represent a significant increase from Louisiana's average of one death annually over the previous 10 years; about one in five infected people die from the infection.
Rising water temperatures caused by climate change are contributing to infection risks in new regions, with Vibrio vulnificus detected this spring in coastal waters near New York's Long Island.
title: Flesh-Eating Bacteria Kills 5 in Louisiana as Cases Surge Past Decade Average

summary: House Democrats are developing a broad investigative strategy targeting companies and financial firms surrounding President Donald Trump , prioritizing evidence-building over immediate impeachment.
Party leaders aim to avoid repeating Trump's first term, when impeachment proceedings consumed Congress and allowed him to cast himself as a victim of partisan attacks.

Representatives Robert Garcia from California and Jamie Raskin from Maryland are sending letters to entities including Paramount Skydance, 1789 Capital, and YouTube, which settled a $24.5 million dispute with Trump in September.

Probes into Homeland Security contracts with private prison operator GEO Group and security firm Salus Worldwide Solutions are planned, alongside investigations into Venezuelan oil sales by commodity traders Vitol and Trafigura.

The White House asserted that Trump has worked to thwart the "radical left's agenda" and remains committed to preserving Republican majorities in Congress, stating officials are "prepared to respond to oversight requests, no matter who is in the House or Senate.
title: Democrats plan Trump investigations over impeachment if they win House: Reuters

bias: Center-Leaning coverage frames the Michigan Senate dispute as a political clash, using phrases such as “fires back” and “slam” while briefly emphasizing Vance’s criticism of El-Sayed’s suitability.

Right-Leaning coverage intensifies the confrontation, repeating “crazy,” “odd,” “lefty,” and “terrible senator,” portraying Vance as answering personal attacks—particularly alleged remarks about his children and “sucking up to power”—rather than launching an unsolicited assault.
The pivotal divide is whether the episode is primarily partisan name-calling or a justified response to a radical opponent; policy proposals and qualifications are de-emphasized by both.
Both perspectives agree Vance attacked El-Sayed during the Michigan race, reflecting broader polarization over civility, identity, and political legitimacy.
summary: Vice President JD Vance criticized Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, calling him "crazy" and predicting he would be a terrible senator for Michigan.
El-Sayed mocked Vance's charisma and made controversial remarks about Vance's children during a podcast.
Vance responded by pointing out that El-Sayed focused on personal insults rather than discussing policies to help Michigan residents.
El-Sayed won the Democratic primary in Michigan and will compete against former Rep. Mike Rogers in the 2026 Midterm elections.
title: JD Vance Criticizes Michigan Senate Candidate Abdul El-Sayed After Verbal Exchange

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the ruling as a major ideological defeat: HUD’s “dramatic” “overhaul” allegedly shifts roughly $4 billion from permanent housing to temporary services, while “walloped,” “ MAGA ,” “slush fund,” and “crusade” cast the effort as partisan and improper.
Center coverage de-emphasizes that broader motive, focusing on procedural invalidity, paused Louisiana applications, and potential jeopardy for nearly 1,800 Arizona residents.
The pivotal divide is whether this is ideological retrenchment or an administrative process failure.
Both emphasize the court’s intervention and funding stakes, reflecting wider tensions over government responsibility, housing policy, and trust in the Trump administration.
summary: On Friday, U.S. District Judge Mary McElroy blocked the Department of Housing and Urban Development from overhauling the $4 billion Continuum of Care program, ruling the agency acted in a "procedurally invalid manner."

HUD Secretary Scott Turner sought to shift funds away from permanent "Housing First" models toward temporary shelters requiring sobriety or treatment, claiming the existing system fueled a " homelessness crisis."

The ruling halts distribution for 450 CoC programs, leaving billions in funding in limbo while advocates estimate the scrapped overhaul could have jeopardized housing assistance for roughly 170,000 vulnerable individuals.

Washington Attorney General Nick Brown and 21 other states filed the lawsuit, marking the third time this year federal judges have invalidated the agency's attempts to bypass standard public comment processes.
Local organizations like UNITY now await federal guidance to determine how to proceed with grant applications while managing services without the anticipated funding distribution rules in place.
title: Judge blocks HUD move to change funding for homelessness programs

bias: Left-Leaning coverage emphasizes the seriousness of Biden’s illness while noting his continued public engagement and Hunter Biden ’s claim that addiction harmed the family.

Right-Leaning coverage intensifies vulnerability through phrases such as “very debilitating,” “aggressive form,” “former Democrat,” and “reveals,” while foregrounding addiction and portraying the pardon as a mistake—an interpretation attributed to some reports, not established fact.

Center coverage leans toward emotional language such as “heartbreaking” and “sad to watch.” Across perspectives, “spread,” bone metastasis, pain, and suffering dominate, with little independent medical confirmation, revealing shared concern filtered through differing priorities about empathy, accountability, and public fitness.
summary: In a BBC Newsnight interview broadcast Friday, Hunter Biden grew emotional discussing former President Joe Biden 's prostate cancer, stating it has metastasized to his bones and is "really sad to watch."

Joe Biden's office announced the diagnosis in May 2025 after urinary symptoms revealed a small nodule on his prostate, characterized by a Gleason score of 9 and metastasis to the bone—an aggressive form of the disease.

Former First Lady Jill Biden recently explained that her husband requires testing every three months and will live with the cancer permanently; she noted "he's doing OK" despite the metastasis to his bones.
Despite his health condition, Hunter claimed his father remains active, "speaking publicly about the issues that are important to him" and continues to believe strongly in the country.

Hunter also addressed his past battle with addiction, describing it as "hell on earth" and noting he "wasnt reaching for anything except oblivion" during that period, contrasting his recovery with his father's current struggle.
title: Hunter Biden says his father’s prostate cancer is causing him pain even as he continues to speak out

bias: Coverage shares the core: Andrew and Tristan Tate are detained in Miami, contesting UK extradition over rape and trafficking allegations, while lawyers argue their visibility makes flight unlikely.

Left-Leaning reports frame this as a “desperate bid,” “too famous to run,” and a “manosphere” influencer’s potential liability for Trump among young male voters, using mocking “roasting” language; the brothers’ denials are noted there.
Right-Leaning coverage foregrounds release, detention, sovereignty, Romanian complications, and the UK’s September 16 document deadline, with restrained liberty-focused rhetoric.
Center coverage stays procedural, emphasizing bail and “serious charges,” revealing broader cultural and geopolitical divides.
summary: Social media influencers Andrew Tate and Tristan Tate remain in a Miami jail while contesting a United Kingdom extradition request linked to 59 charges, including rape and human trafficking.
The Trump administration previously pressured Romanian authorities to lift travel restrictions on the brothers, enabling their departure after a 2022 arrest on similar allegations.

Lawyer Joseph McBride warned that President Donald Trump risks alienating young male voters if refusing to intervene, claiming "Andrew Tate was a material participant in ensuring President Trump's victory."
White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt ruled out intervention with a simple "no," while Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated, "There's no role for us to play at this moment."

Scholar Sidney Blumenthal and journalist Nina Burleigh argue the case signals a significant scandal, describing the brothers' network as "the greatest international crime syndicate with the greatest political influence in history.
title: Defense attorneys say Tate brothers should remain free in the US as they fight extradition to the UK

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Greg Abel’s move as the symbolic release of Buffett’s “massive cash hoard,” while tempering enthusiasm by noting Berkshire still lagged the S&P 500 and insurance weakened.

Right-Leaning coverage celebrates a “staggering investment,” “cash hoarding” ending, $4.5 billion buybacks, and a “buy zone,” portraying decisive leadership after the “post-Warren Buffett hangover.” Center coverage emphasizes the strategic shift, precise 16% earnings growth to roughly $13 billion, and broader purchases, including a $6.8 billion deal and over $24 billion in stocks.
All highlight reduced cash, the $10 billion Alphabet investment, and stronger operations, reflecting debates over stewardship, shareholder returns, and market confidence.
summary: On Saturday, Berkshire Hathaway reported second-quarter operating earnings climbed 16% to $12.98 billion as CEO Greg Abel began deploying cash, which shrank to $365.5 billion from $397.4 billion.

Abel is accelerating capital deployment, marking a shift from the net-selling strategy Berkshire maintained for 14 consecutive quarters before becoming a net buyer of equities with nearly $20 billion in purchases.
Alphabet Inc. joined Berkshire's top five equity holdings after a $10 billion investment to support artificial intelligence, placing it alongside longtime stakes in Apple and Coca-Cola.
Repurchasing approximately $4.5 billion of its own shares during the quarter, Berkshire provided shareholders with the largest quarterly payout since 2021, followed by over $3.3 billion in July.

In July, Berkshire completed a $6.8 billion acquisition of homebuilder Taylor Morrison Home Corp., demonstrating Abel's strategy of utilizing cash reserves to expand the conglomerate's diverse business portfolio.
title: Berkshire earnings rose last quarter and CEO Greg Abel is starting to deploy Buffett’s massive cash hoard

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames California’s proposed $5,000-per-violation penalties as a bid to “strengthen electoral transparency,” while acknowledging burdens on small creators; right-leaning coverage foregrounds government punishment and casts nondisclosure as “hiding” campaign payments, with “Paid to persuade?” inviting suspicion.
Center coverage sits between them, using conditional language such as “may” while noting the emerging advertising issue and legal costs.
The pivotal divide is whether disclosure protects voters or constrains political speech, especially for influencers like Shaka Smith, whose 700,000-plus followers magnify influence.
All emphasize paid political posts, potential fines, and accountability, reflecting broader regulatory-versus-free-expression tensions.
summary: Democratic Assemblymember Marc Berman proposed legislation to penalize content creators who fail to disclose paid political endorsements, empowering the Fair Political Practices Commission to issue fines up to $5,000 per violation.
Along with Texas, California is one of two states with disclosure mandates for paid political posts, while similar bills failed in recent years in Utah and Georgia.
Los Angeles-based influencer Shaka Smith disclosed his payment from Tom Steyer's campaign to his more than 700,000 followers, though other creators allegedly failed to reveal similar arrangements.
Southern California-based creator Dustin Torreverde worries new penalties place unfair financial burden on smaller influencers , as current enforcement via court order can take months to obtain.

Federal disclosure rules for political content do not exist, though California Sen. Adam Schiff introduced legislation last month as outside groups urge the Federal Election Commission to establish national standards.
title: California may fine content creators who don’t disclose they were paid to post about politics

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the SAVE America Act as a voter-access threat, saying millions could be disenfranchised and voters were “spared,” while describing Trump’s push to “nuke” the filibuster and Blanche as a “personal servant.” Right-leaning coverage casts the same proof-of-citizenship measure as an “election-integrity bill,” Trump’s “#1 legislative demand,” and the Senate’s departure as having “left town,” a failure of leadership.
Center coverage emphasizes a “crushing standoff,” procedural postponement, funding, and Blanche’s confirmation.
All agree the bill stalled, funding passed, and Blanche was confirmed, reflecting broader divides over election security, voting access, executive influence, and institutional norms.
summary: Senate Republicans departed for summer recess, ending a standoff over President Donald Trump's demand to abolish the legislative filibuster and pass the SAVE America Act, a strict proof-of-citizenship voting bill.

For weeks, Trump pressured Senate Majority Leader John Thune to abandon the 60-vote threshold, but the SAVE America Act lacked sufficient support among the slim Republican majority, who resisted changing the chamber's rules.

Following a late-night call with the president, Sen. Ron Johnson, Sen. Mike Lee, and Sen. Rick Scott announced an alternative plan: attaching voting bill elements to a broader budget package for the Pentagon when the Senate returns in September.

During the 20-hour session, Thune confirmed Attorney General Todd Blanche, passed Russian sanctions, and approved a government funding package, despite managing a slim majority with Sen. Mitch McConnell absent.
The standoff illustrates Trump's ongoing struggle to master the Senate, where established rules and slim margins continue to constrain his legislative agenda despite his de facto speaker ambitions.
title: Senators head for the exits without meeting Trump’s demands for voting bill
